To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
chronic corticosterone administration decreases type II corticosterone receptors in the hippocampal and frontal cortex and in circulating lymphocytes.

the regulation of corticosterone receptors in the hippocampal formation, frontal cortex, pituitary, circulating lymphocytes, spleens, thymus and hypothalamus are differentially regulated in a tissue specific manner.

chronic stress, chronic corticosterone administration, and acute stress all increase hippocampal glucocorticoid (GC) receptor levels, while chronic corticosterone and acute stress decrease hippocampal mineralocorticoid receptor levels.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of corticosteroids in the regulation of brain and immune function.
the regulation of brain corticoster-oid receptors in response both to changes in circulating corticosteroid levels and to stress.
the role of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis in the regulation of immune function and the mechanisms by which glucocorticoids regulate immune function.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
corticosteroid regulation is tissue specific, and that there is a lack of correlation between corticosterone regulation of receptors and receptor type (i.e. type I vs. type II).
the regulation of brain corticosteroids is not the same as lymphoid corticosterone regulation.
the regulation of corticosterone receptors by corticosteroids is complex and tissue specific, with the hippocampus and circulating lymphocytes showing a similar pattern of regulation.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

corticosterone downregulates glucocorticoid but not mineralocorticoid receptor levels in hippocampal and frontal cortical neurons, but that it does not alter glucocorticoid or mineralocorticoid levels in the pituitary or lymphoid tissue.
the hippocampus is a very special case in the brain, and that the hippocampus and the lymphocytes are very similar in their corticosterone regulation.
the hippocampal type II receptors were the most sensitive to changes in circulating corticosteroid levels.
The main takeaway from our work is that
corticosteroid regulation is not uniform across tissues.
there are differences in the regulation of glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid receptor expression in the hippocampus and frontal cortex.
there is a complex regulation of corticosterone receptors, and that the regulation of corticosteorid receptors in lymphoid tissues is different than that in brain.
